Problem representation: A 40‑year‑old man with multiple sclerosis on ocrelizumab for 10.6 years presents five weeks after his last infusion with a new respiratory illness, low IgG (422 mg/dL), HRCT ground‑glass and peripheral migratory consolidation, and BAL showing 70 % lymphocytes.

Assessment: Drug‑related inflammatory lung disease is plausible; ocrelizumab has been linked to interstitial lung disease and organizing pneumonia, and prolonged B‑cell depletion can cause hypogammaglobulinemia that predisposes to infection. The marked BAL lymphocytosis favors a hypersensitivity or viral process rather than typical bacterial pneumonia. Infectious causes remain possible despite negative SARS‑CoV‑2; PJP, CMV, atypical bacteria, fungi, and mycobacteria can produce similar imaging and lymphocytic BAL, especially in the setting of IgG < 500 mg/dL.

Required work‑up before attribution: quantitative immunoglobulins (IgG, IgA, IgM), serum KL‑6 and surfactant protein‑D, autoantibody panel, comprehensive BAL microbiology (bacterial, fungal, mycobacterial cultures, PJP PCR, viral panel), and consideration of transbronchial or surgical lung biopsy for histopathology. Pulmonary function testing and review of prior infusion reactions should also be documented. Only after excluding infection and confirming a drug‑related pattern can a decision on ocrelizumab continuation or immunosuppression be made promptly
